date.label: Undated Deuteronomic discourse and legislation
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: Moses commands the appointment of judges and officers "in all thy gates… throughout thy tribes," to judge the people "with just judgment" (16:18).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 16:18, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). *Mišpaṭ-ṣedeq* ("just judgment") is BDB H4941 sense 1–2 (read in full).

claims.claim: The judge is forbidden to wrest judgment, to respect persons, and to take a gift, "for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous" (16:19).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 16:19, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). BDB H4941 sense 5 cites Deut 16:19 for "wrest right." Parallel: Ex 23:8; Lev 19:15; Deut 1:17.

claims.claim: The command is positive as well as negative: "That which is altogether just shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live, and inherit the land" (16:20) — justice is tied to life and land.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 16:20, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Verses 16:21–22 prohibit planting a grove (*ʾăšērâ*) near the altar and setting up a pillar (*maṣṣēbâ*), "which the LORD thy God hateth."
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 16:21–22, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The gate was the place of public resort where business was transacted and causes decided, so "judges in all thy gates" means a decentralised local judiciary.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 16:18 (read in full: "the gate was the place of public resort… where business was transacted and causes decided"). Corroborated by Ruth 4:1–11; 2 Sam 15:2 (cited by BDB at H4941 sense 1).

claims.claim: The officers (*šōṭĕrîm*) were the heralds or bailiffs who executed the judges' sentences.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 16:18 (read in full: "officers — heralds or bailiffs, employed in executing the sentence of their superiors"). Same officers reappear in Deut 20:5–9.

claims.claim: No animal with any blemish or evil favour is to be sacrificed to the LORD; it is an abomination (17:1).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:1, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: An idolatry case — serving other gods, "either the sun, or moon, or any of the host of heaven" — requires a report, a hearing, and diligent inquiry, and is punished only "if it be true, and the thing certain" (17:2–4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:2–4, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). The inquiry language ("enquire diligently") recurs at 19:18.

claims.claim: The convicted idolater is stoned at the gates; the hands of the witnesses are first upon him, and then the hands of all the people (17:5–7).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:5–7, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). JFB on 17:6–7: the witnesses' priority "was calculated to deter men from being rash in accusing."

claims.claim: No one is put to death on the testimony of one witness; "at the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, shall he that is worthy of death be put to death" (17:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Same rule at Deut 19:15; Num 35:30.

claims.claim: A matter "too hard" for local judgment — "between blood and blood, between plea and plea, and between stroke and stroke" — is taken up to the chosen place, to "the priests the Levites, and unto the judge that shall be in those days" (17:8–9).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:8–9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). The three pairs cover homicide, civil suits, and assault (JFB, read in full).

claims.claim: JFB identifies the central tribunal with the later Sanhedrin ("the Sanhedrim — the supreme council, which was composed partly of civil and partly of ecclesiastical persons"). The identification is JFB's retrospective label; the text names only priests, Levites, and the judge.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 17:8–13 (read in full). The term "Sanhedrin" is Second Temple usage; the dossier records the identification as a traditional commentary reading, not as the text's own term.

claims.claim: The tribunal's sentence is binding — "thou shalt not decline from the sentence… to the right hand, nor to the left" — and the man who acts presumptuously and will not hearken to priest or judge "shall die" (17:10–13).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:10–13, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The king law is triggered by the people's future request — "I will set a king over me, like as all the nations that are about me" — and is a provision for that request, not a command to appoint a king (17:14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). JFB on 17:14–20 (read in full): "No sanction or recommendation was indicated; on the contrary… the divine disapproval was expressed in the most unequivocal terms (1 Sam 8:7)."

claims.claim: The king must be God-chosen and "one from among thy brethren"; "thou mayest not set a stranger over thee" (17:15).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The king must not multiply horses, nor cause the people to return to Egypt for horses; must not multiply wives "that his heart turn not away"; and must not "greatly multiply to himself silver and gold" (17:16–17).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:16–17, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The king must write "a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites," keep it with him, and read it all the days of his life, to learn to fear the LORD and keep the law (17:18–19).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:18–19, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The stated purpose of the king's daily reading is humility and longevity: "that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren… to the end that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he, and his children, in the midst of Israel" (17:20).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:20, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: *Mišpaṭ* (H4941) spans the act of judging, the ordinance, and the priest's due: BDB sense 3 cites 1 Sam 8:9, 11 and 1 Sam 10:25 as "law of king," and sense 5 cites Deut 18:3 for the priest's due. The king law's vocabulary is therefore the same vocabulary as the judiciary and the priesthood.
claims.evidence: BDB H4941 (read in full via BibleHub).

claims.claim: *Mišneh hattôrâ* (17:18) means "a copy of this law," not a second, distinct law; the LXX's rendering *to deuteronomion touto* ("this Second Law") is the origin of the book's Greek name, Deuteronomy.
claims.evidence: NET Bible note on Deut 17:18 (read via BibleGateway search excerpts: "the MT's expression *mishneh hattorah hazzoʾt* is better rendered 'copy of this law'"); TheTorah.com, "The Second Torah" (read in full, published 2025-09-29): LXX renders *to deuteronomion touto*; "the Greek translation's rendition of 'mishneh' as 'second' is likely what gave the book its name."

claims.claim: The extent of "this law" in 17:18 is debated: the NET note says *tôrâ* here "probably refers only to Deuteronomy, not to the whole Pentateuch"; whether it is the king law pericope, the Deuteronomic code, or the whole Torah is not settled by the text alone.
claims.evidence: NET Bible note on Deut 17:18 (search excerpts). The debate is recorded, not resolved.

claims.claim: Levinson's thesis — Deuteronomy reconceptualises kingship by stripping the king of military, judicial, cultic, and patronage power and subordinating him to the Torah and the Levitical priests, and the Deuteronomistic History then subverts that programme by celebrating kingly power — is presented as a scholarly reading, not as established fact, because Levinson 2001 was not read directly. Berman's framing (the king's limits are "without parallel in the ancient Near East") rests on the same second-hand basis.
claims.evidence: Levinson 2001, *Vetus Testamentum* 51.4: 511–34 — **not read directly**; via the Augsburg Fortress introduction (PDF, search excerpts) and the Stellenbosch thesis (search excerpts, citing Levinson 2001:512). Berman, *Created Equal* — **not read directly**; via search excerpts. Both second-hand sources are named; the claim is capped at Probable.

claims.claim: Solomon breached the three limits of Deut 17:16–17 in the narrative's own terms: 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen with horses "brought out of Egypt" (1 Kgs 10:26–29), and 700 wives and 300 concubines, "his wives turned away his heart" (1 Kgs 11:1–4).
claims.evidence: KJV 1 Kgs 10:26–29; 11:1–4, read via BibleGateway search excerpts; exact wording on record. JFB on Deut 17:14–20 (read in full) notes the breach was "exemplified in the history of Solomon and other princes."

claims.claim: Josephus adds to the Deuteronomic polity what the text does not contain: seven judges per city with two Levite officers each, and a king who acts only with the high priest and "the votes of the senators." These are Josephus' systematisation, not Deuteronomy's text.
claims.evidence: Josephus, *Ant.* 4.8 §§1–14 (read in full; "Let there be seven men to judge in every city… Let every judge have two officers allotted him out of the tribe of Levi"); the king and senate (via *browser.find* excerpts, §§15–16 — access level: excerpts only, so the claim is capped at Probable).

claims.claim: The priests the Levites, the whole tribe of Levi, "shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel: they shall eat the offerings of the LORD made by fire, and his inheritance… the LORD is their inheritance" (18:1–2).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:1–2, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Parallel: Deut 10:8–9.

claims.claim: The priest's due from the people is specified: "the shoulder, and the two cheeks, and the maw" from ox or sheep; the firstfruit of corn, wine, and oil; "the first of the fleece of thy sheep" (18:3–4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:3–4, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). BDB H4941 sense 5 cites Deut 18:3 for "due of the priests." JFB (read in full) notes the uncertainty whether this is new or a repetition with more detail (Lev 7:31–33 gives breast and shoulder).

claims.claim: The LORD "hath chosen him out of all thy tribes, to stand to minister in the name of the LORD, him and his sons for ever" (18:5).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:5, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: A Levite who comes "with all the desire of his mind" to the chosen place ministers there as all his brethren do, with "like portions to eat, beside that which cometh of the sale of his patrimony" (18:6–8).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:6–8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). JFB (read in full): the Levites served in rotation; the zealous Levite is admitted to full participation.

claims.claim: The nations' abominations are listed and forbidden: child sacrifice, divination, observer of times, enchanter, witch, charmer, consulter with familiar spirits, wizard, necromancer (18:10–11).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:10–11, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The positive command after the list: "Thou shalt be perfect with the LORD thy God" (18:13) — the nations hearken to diviners, but "as for thee, the LORD thy God hath not suffered thee so to do" (18:14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:13–14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken" (18:15).
claims.evidence: BDB H5030 sense 1 cites Deut 18:15, 18 as "prophet like Moses." The verbatim quotation in the claim is KJV Deut 18:15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The promise answers the Horeb request — "Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I die not" (18:16) — which the LORD approves: "They have well spoken" (18:17).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:16–17, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The prophet's commission: "I will put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak unto them all that I shall command him" (18:18); disobedience carries the sanction "I will require it of him" (18:19).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:18–19, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The false prophet — one who presumes to speak a word the LORD has not commanded, or speaks in the name of other gods — "even that prophet shall die" (18:20).
claims.evidence: BDB H5030 sense 2 cites Deut 18:20, 22 for false prophets. The verbatim quotation in the claim ("even that prophet shall die") is KJV Deut 18:20, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The test of a prophet: "when a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken… thou shalt not be afraid of him" (18:21–22).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:21–22, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: *Nābîʾ* (H5030) means "spokesman, speaker, prophet"; BDB's entry cites Deut 18:15, 18 for the genuine prophet "like Moses" and Deut 18:20, 22 for the false prophet.
claims.evidence: BDB H5030 (read in full via BibleHub).

claims.claim: JFB reads the prophet promise doubly: it applies to the succession of true prophets God commissioned, and "pre-eminently the Messiah, for He alone was 'like unto Moses' in His mediatorial character… in the number, variety, and magnitude of His miracles; in His close and familiar communion with God; and in His being the author of a new dispensation."
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 18:15–19 (read in full). The double reading is JFB's interpretation; it is recorded as a traditional reading, not as the text's plain statement.

claims.claim: Whether the promise refers to a succession of prophets, to a single eschatological prophet, or to both is Debated. The New Testament's application to Jesus (Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37) is an application, not a resolution of the Deuteronomic referent.
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 18:15–19 (read in full, double reading); the Acts texts (read in full, see clm-deu-05-039/040). The debate is recorded, not resolved.

claims.claim: Acts 3:22–23 is an adaptation of Deut 18:15 + 18:19, not a verbatim quotation. Peter says "A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you" — combining 18:15 ("like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken") with 18:19 ("whosoever will not hearken… I will require it of him") — and renders the sanction as "every soul, which will not hear that prophet, shall be destroyed from among the people" (3:23). The wording differs from Deuteronomy at both points.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:15, 19, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); Acts 3:22–23, read in full via BibleGateway KJV pages. Wording comparison: Deut 18:15 "unto him ye shall hearken" / Acts 3:22 "him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you"; Deut 18:19 "I will require it of him" / Acts 3:23 "shall be destroyed from among the people." See also rejected connection R1. Comparison re-verified against the gateway KJV text, 2026-11-20; the wording differences hold unchanged.

claims.claim: Acts 7:37 is a close quotation of Deut 18:15 with reordering: "This is that Moses, which said unto the children of Israel, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear." The Deuteronomic wording is preserved ("A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me") with the addressee shifted from second person ("unto thee") to third person ("unto you").
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 18:15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); Acts 7:37, read in full via BibleGateway KJV pages. Comparison re-verified against the gateway KJV text, 2026-11-20; the close quotation and the second-to-third-person shift hold unchanged.

claims.claim: Three cities of refuge are to be separated in the midst of the land, with roads prepared and the land divided into three parts, "that every slayer may flee thither" (19:1–3).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:1–3, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The case is the unintentional slayer — one who kills his neighbour "ignorantly, whom he hated not in time past" — exemplified by the axe-head slipping from the helve in the wood and killing a neighbour; "he shall flee unto one of those cities, and live" (19:4–5).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:4–5, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The reason is the avenger of blood: "lest the avenger of the blood pursue the slayer, while his heart is hot, and overtake him, because the way is long, and slay him; whereas he was not worthy of death" (19:6).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:6, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). JFB on 19:2 (read in full): *goelism* — "the duty of the nearest kinsmen to avenge the death of a slaughtered relative" — was "incorporated… in an improved form" by Moses.

claims.claim: Three more cities are conditional: "if the LORD thy God enlarge thy coast… and thou shalt keep all these commandments to do them" (19:8–9). JFB notes the condition was never fulfilled — "the three other cities were never added, because the people did not fulfil the conditions on which the promise of their establishment was suspended" — and reads the whole institution as "an express type of the gospel."
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:8–9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). JFB on 19:8–9 (read in full) for the never-added point and the typological reading. The typological reading is JFB's, not the text's.

claims.claim: The stated purpose is that "innocent blood be not shed in thy land" (19:10).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:10, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The deliberate murderer — one who hates his neighbour, lies in wait, and smites him mortally — is fetched by "the elders of his city" from the city of refuge and delivered to the avenger; "thine eye shall not pity him" (19:11–13).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:11–13, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set" (19:14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Parallel: Deut 27:17 ("cursed be he that removeth his neighbour's landmark").

claims.claim: One witness is insufficient: "at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established" (19:15).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Parallel: Deut 17:6; Num 35:30; Matt 18:16; 2 Cor 13:1; John 8:17; 1 Tim 5:19.

claims.claim: The false witness stands with the accused "before the LORD, before the priests and the judges"; the judges make "diligent inquisition"; if the witness testified falsely, "then shall ye do unto him, as he had thought to have done unto his brother" (19:16–19).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:16–19, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). JFB on 19:16–19 (read in full): "if convicted of perjury, it will be sufficient for his own condemnation, and his punishment shall be exactly the same as would have overtaken the object of his malignant prosecution."

claims.claim: The talionic formula: "Thine eye shall not pity; but life shall go for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot" (19:21).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:21, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Parallel: Ex 21:23–25; Lev 24:19–20. Hammurabi §§196–214 comparison reused from the Exodus covenant dossier §5.2 (verified read there).

claims.claim: Deuteronomy 19 states the refuge institution without the two features of Numbers 35: the congregation's trial (Num 35:12, 24–25) and the term of exile until the death of the high priest (Num 35:25, 28, 32). The omission is a textual fact; why Deuteronomy omits them is Debated.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 19:1–13, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); Num 35:6–34 via BibleGateway search excerpts: the slayer "shall stand before the congregation in judgment" (35:12), the congregation "shall deliver the slayer" and he "shall abide in it unto the death of the high priest" (35:24–25, 28), and "no satisfaction" is taken to return early (35:32)). The reason for the difference is not stated by either text. Comparison re-verified against the gateway KJV text, 2026-11-20; Deut 19:1–13 contains neither feature and the Num 35 wording is as quoted.

claims.claim: "When thou goest out to battle against thine enemies, and seest horses, and chariots, and a people more than thou, be not afraid of them: for the LORD thy God is with thee, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt" (20:1). The exodus is the ground of courage in war.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 20:1, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The priest approaches the people before battle and speaks: "let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble, neither be ye terrified… for the LORD your God is he that goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you" (20:2–4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 20:2–4, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The officers exempt three classes before battle: the man who has built a new house and not dedicated it, who has planted a vineyard and not yet eaten of it, and who has betrothed a wife and not taken her — each "lest he die in the battle, and another man" take his place (20:5–7).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 20:5–7, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). JFB on 20:5–7 (read in full) gives the rationale for each: the house, the vineyard, and the wife are all begun enterprises that the man should complete.

claims.claim: The fearful and fainthearted are exempt — "lest his brethren's heart faint as well as his heart" (20:8) — and only then "the officers shall… make captains of the armies to lead the people" (20:9). The exemptions come before the appointment of commanders.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 20:8–9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). JFB on 20:5–9 (read in full): the officers are the *Shoterim*.

claims.claim: Before a distant city is fought, peace is proclaimed: "When thou comest nigh unto a city to fight against it, then proclaim peace unto it" (20:10). A city that answers peace "shall be tributaries unto thee, and they shall serve thee" (20:11).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 20:10–11, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: A city that refuses peace is besieged, and "thou shalt smite every male thereof with the edge of the sword: but the women, and the little ones, and the cattle, and all that is in the city… shalt thou take unto thyself" (20:12–14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 20:12–14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The two treatments are distinguished by distance: "thus shalt thou do unto all the cities which are very far off from thee, which are not of the cities of these nations" (20:15).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 20:15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: For the cities of the inheritance the command is total: "thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth: but thou shalt utterly destroy them; namely, the Hittites, and the Amorites, the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites" (20:16–17).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 20:16–17, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). BDB H2764 (read in full) cites Deut 20:17 among the ban passages.

claims.claim: The text gives its own rationale: "that they teach you not to do after all their abominations, which they have done unto their gods; so should ye sin against the LORD your God" (20:18).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 20:18, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: In a long siege, fruit trees are spared: "thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by forcing an axe against them: for thou mayest eat of them… (for the tree of the field is man's life)"; only trees "which thou knowest that they be not trees for meat" may be cut for bulwarks (20:19–20).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 20:19–20, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). JFB on 20:19–20 (read in full) notes the fruit trees' preservation as a provision for the conqueror's sustenance.

claims.claim: *Ḥērem* (H2764) is "devotion, ban" — a thing devoted to the LORD, hostile to theocracy and therefore to be destroyed or set apart to sacred uses; the same word has a sanctuary side ("every *ḥērem* is most holy to the LORD," Lev 27:28) and a lethal side (Deut 20:17).
claims.evidence: BDB H2764 (read in full via BibleHub).

claims.claim: The herem of Deut 20:16–18 requires four separate analyses — rhetoric (the totality language), lethal semantics (the ban as BDB defines it), historicity (what happened, as against what the text commands), and ethical appraisal — and must not be made harmless by an assertion of hyperbole. This is the Phase 2 correction applied to this category; the canonical treatment is the shared record `verification/shared/herem-warfare-ethics.md` (Category 3 owner), which does not yet exist, so this dossier states the four analyses for Deut 20:16–18 only and cross-references the shared record as pending.
claims.evidence: Coordinator Brief; Phase 2 Final Report (documented error: warfare/herem); BDB H2764 (read in full). See §5.4.

claims.claim: The priest who addresses the army (20:2–4) is identified by JFB as a priest "appointed to this duty" by a special ceremony, sounding the trumpets (Num 10:9; 31:6) and consulting the Urim (Num 27:21); Josephus places the high priest alongside the king in counsel (Ant. 4.8, via find excerpts). The identification is a commentary reconstruction, not the text's own statement (the text says only "the priest shall approach and speak").
claims.evidence: JFB on Deut 20:2–4 (read in full: "a priest… was appointed to this duty, with a special ceremonial… the war trumpets were sounded"); Josephus, *Ant.* 4.8, king passage (via *browser.find* excerpts — access level: excerpts only). Capped at Probable.

claims.claim: There is no direct archaeological evidence in this session for the institutions of this category as described — the cities of refuge, the central tribunal, the king's copy of the law, the war priest, or the herem's execution — and no site in this range is identified by inscription. The gate complexes are the architectural context for local judgment, not evidence for the law.
claims.evidence: No excavation report was consulted in this session; the negative finding is stated as such (Standards §3.1). See §6.

claims.claim: Prescribed law and attested practice diverge in the narratives: the law limits the king's horses, wives, and wealth (17:16–17), while Solomon multiplies them (1 Kgs 10:26–29; 11:1–4); the law gives the prophet a fulfilment test (18:21–22), while the narratives show false prophets prospering for a time; the law commands the herem (20:16–17), while the narratives show the nations surviving (Josh 9; Judg 1–2). The divergence is the finding; the dossier does not harmonise it away.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 17:16–17; 18:21–22; 20:16–17, read in full (BibleGateway KJV); 1 Kgs 10:26–29; 11:1–4 (read via BibleGateway search excerpts). See §3.6.

connections.note: Moses sits to judge and appoints rulers over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens (Ex 18:13–27); the Deuteronomic judges in the gates are the same decentralised judiciary, now commanded for every town. Ex 18:13–27 within Ex 18 (27 verses).

The charge to the judges: "hear the causes between your brethren, and judge righteously… ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God's." Deut 1:16–17 within Deut 1 (46 verses).
Ex 23:8: "thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous" — near-verbatim with Deut 16:19. Ex 23:1–9 within Ex 23 (33 verses).

"Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour." Lev 19:15 within Lev 19 (37 verses).

"But ye shall destroy their altars, break their images, and cut down their groves." Ex 34:13 within Ex 34 (35 verses). The grove and pillar beside the altar (Deut 16:21–22) are the same abominations the exodus law commands to destroy.

"He that sacrificeth unto any god, save unto the LORD only, he shall be utterly destroyed." Ex 22:20 within Ex 22 (31 verses). The capital idolatry procedure of Deut 17:2–7 applies the same principle with procedural safeguards.

The two-or-three-witnesses rule of 17:6 is restated in 19:15 ("at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established"). Internal restatement within the same category.

Jehoshaphat "set judges in the land throughout all the fenced cities of Judah, city by city," and in Jerusalem set priests, Levites, and heads of families "for the judgment of the LORD, and for controversies" — the closest attested practice to the Deuteronomic central tribunal. 2 Chron 19:4–11 within 2 Chron 19 (11 verses). Not a proof that Jehoshaphat was implementing Deut 17.

The elders request a king "like as all the nations"; the LORD says "they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them" (8:7); Samuel shows "the manner of the king" (8:11–18). The narrative fulfilment of Deut 17:14. 1 Sam 8:4–22 within 1 Sam 8 (22 verses).

Samuel calls the people to Mizpeh, Saul is chosen by lot, and Samuel "told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote it in a book, and laid it up before the LORD" (10:25) — the only narrative instance of a king's law written in a book, echoing Deut 17:18. 1 Sam 10:17–25 within 1 Sam 10 (27 verses).

Solomon "gathered together chariots and horsemen: and he had a thousand and four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen… and Solomon had horses brought out of Egypt" — the exact breach of Deut 17:16. 1 Kgs 10:26–29 within 1 Kgs 10 (29 verses).
Solomon "had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart" — the exact breach of Deut 17:17. 1 Kgs 11:1–4 within 1 Kgs 11 (43 verses).

Hilkiah finds "the book of the law in the house of the LORD"; Josiah rends his clothes and sends to inquire of the LORD — the law, found and read, driving the reform. 2 Kgs 22:8–13 within 2 Kgs 22 (20 verses).

"Moses wrote this law, and delivered it unto the priests the sons of Levi… and unto all the elders of Israel," to be read to all Israel every seven years (31:9–13). The king's personal copy and the public reading are the same practice in two places. Deut 31:9–13 within Deut 31 (30 verses).

"At that time the LORD separated the tribe of Levi… wherefore Levi hath no part nor inheritance with his brethren; the LORD is his inheritance, according as the LORD thy God promised him." Deut 10:8–9 within Deut 10 (22 verses).

"They which minister about holy things live of the things of the temple; and they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar. Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel." Paul's reuse of the priest's-due principle. 1 Cor 9:13–14 within 1 Cor 9 (27 verses).

Peter applies the promise to Jesus: "A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you. And it shall come to pass, that every soul, which will not hear that prophet, shall be destroyed from among the people." An adaptation combining 18:15 and 18:19 — see clm-deu-05-039 and rejected connection R1. Acts 3:22–23 within Acts 3 (26 verses).

Stephen: "This is that Moses, which said unto the children of Israel, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear." A close quotation with reordering — see clm-deu-05-040. Acts 7:37 within Acts 7 (60 verses).

"And they asked him, What then? Art thou Elias? And he saith, I am not. Art thou that prophet? And he answered, No." The expectation of "that prophet" was live in the first century. John 1:21 within John 1 (51 verses).
"Many of the people therefore, when they heard this saying, said, Of a truth this is the Prophet." John 7:40 within John 7 (53 verses).

"And there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face." The book's closing frame on the promise — the prophet like Moses is not yet arisen when Deuteronomy ends. Deut 34:10 within Deut 34 (12 verses).

The false prophet test: a prophet or dreamer whose sign comes to pass but who says "let us go after other gods" is not hearkened to, and "that prophet… shall be put to death." The companion criterion to 18:20–22 — fulfilment alone is not enough. Deut 13:1–5 within Deut 13 (18 verses).

The fuller legislation: six cities of refuge (three east, three in Canaan), for Israelite, stranger, and sojourner; the slayer "shall stand before the congregation in judgment" (35:12); the congregation delivers him and he abides "unto the death of the high priest" (35:24–25, 28); "no satisfaction" to return early (35:32). Deut 19 omits the trial and the term — see clm-deu-05-051. Num 35:9–34 within Num 35 (34 verses).

The implementation: the LORD speaks to Joshua, "Appoint out for you cities of refuge, whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses" (Josh 20:1–2) — the text's own cross-reference to Deuteronomy. Josh 20:1–9 within Josh 20 (9 verses).

"Then Moses severed three cities on this side Jordan toward the sunrising… Bezer in the wilderness… Ramoth in Gilead… and Golan in Bashan" — the eastern three cities, named. Deut 4:41–43 within Deut 4 (49 verses).
"Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour's landmark. And all the people shall say, Amen." Deut 27:17 within Deut 27 (26 verses).
"But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established." Matt 18:16 within Matt 18 (35 verses).
"In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established." 2 Cor 13:1 within 2 Cor 13 (14 verses).
"It is also written in your law, that the testimony of two men is true." John 8:17 within John 8 (59 verses).
"And if any mischief follow, then thou shalt give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot." Ex 21:23–25 within Ex 21 (36 verses).
"And if a man cause a blemish in his neighbour; as he hath done, so shall it be done to him; breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth." Lev 24:19–20 within Lev 24 (23 verses).

"Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: but I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." Matt 5:38–42 within Matt 5 (48 verses).

"And the city shall be accursed, even it, and all that are therein, to the LORD… and they utterly destroyed all that was in the city" — the ban in the conquest narrative. Josh 6:17–21 within Josh 6 (27 verses).

"Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not" — the ban commanded and, in the narrative, incompletely carried out (Saul spares Agag; 1 Sam 15:8–9, 22–23). 1 Sam 15:3 within 1 Sam 15 (35 verses).

"In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes." The refrain that frames the monarchy's absence before the king law's fulfilment. Judg 21:25 within Judg 21 (25 verses).
